title: Jet Lag
full_review:
Strangers thrown together during an extended airport delay reject then reassess each other over the course of a bickering, bantering evening in the French production "Jet Lag" (Miramax).

Already stressed out in the airport bathroom as she juggles clothes and shoulder bags, Rose (Juliette Binoche) accidentally flushes her cell phone into oblivion in mid-conversation. Even her natural beauty and liberally but expertly applied makeup cannot disguise a woman in emotional crisis.

Back at the departure gate it's clear the inclement Parisian weather and a strike action are grounding all flights indefinitely. Expatriate chef Felix (Jean Reno) needs a flight to Munich, hopefully to reconcile with the woman who curtly ditched him in the States.

Rose briefly borrows his cell phone and moves on, but when the next few calls he gets are for Rose he is annoyed he must find her as she was heading to a job in Acapulco. When Felix spots her he quickly discovers she was leaving an abusive lover but is relenting and about to grab a cab home. Instead he suggests she think it over calmly and gallantly offers to share his twin-bedded airport hotel room.

Over a room-service dinner which perfectionist chef Felix scorns, small talk gives way to arch opinions and mutual insults. Felix, still smarting from being dumped, looks down on Rose, criticizing her heavy makeup, especially hurtful as she is an award-winning cosmetician. For her part, Rose gives as good as she gets to the arrogant fusspot who has severed his connection to his French homeland and family.

Animosity, however, gives way to attentive ears as each opens up to the other, sure that they will be in different continents the next day, never to meet again. The emotional Ferris wheel continues its highs and lows even when they are a world apart the next night, wondering if it's still not too late for them to reconnect and make a fresh start.

Directed by Daniele Thompson and co-written with her son, Christopher Thompson, the film is essentially about hope and the possibility of change despite interior attitudes and external obstacles.

Felix are Rose are both at a crossroads, represented by the airport and all the physical and emotional baggage they are carrying. They are literally surrounded by confusion and anxiety at the terminal -- and in themselves.

Rose's makeup has also served to create a shield between her and the people in her life who deride her. When she emerges from a shower in the hotel room, her face fresh-scrubbed, she indicates she is tentatively willing to shed more than powder and goo; she doesn't need to always hide behind a facade.

Through her eyes, Felix realizes perhaps he has been too harsh in cutting off all communication with his demanding but now elderly father. Between the mix of criticism and kindness each offers the other, they are both enabled to take new steps in positive directions -- and possibly toward each other as well.

Yet it is curious that the film is co-written and directed by a woman since Rose's character seems so dependent on having a man at the center of her life to ground her sense of self.
For such a dialogue-heavy film, the quality of the performers is of paramount importance, and Reno and Binoche are up to the task.

Subtitles.

Because of sexual references, a flash of rear nudity and occasional rough language, the USCCB Office for Film & Broadcasting classification is A-III -- adults. The Motion Picture Association of America rating is R -- restricted.
